newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu leaves Zaire, aides say he will return.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu leaves Zaire, aides say he will return.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko left Zaire on Wednesday for a regional summit on the civil war in his troubled country and many people in his capital openly speculated that he had gone for good.
But Mobutu aides insisted that the veteran leader, who has dominated Africa's third largest country for over three decades, would return from the mini-summit in Gabon by Friday.
"He will be back in 24 or 48 hours," presidential spokesman Kabuya Lumuna told Reuters.
Mobutu, battling cancer and Laurent Kabila's rebels, landed in Gabon's capital Libreville with his wife Bobi Ladawa. Witnesses said he looked tired and went straight to a waiting vehicle.
The Zaire government said he was to discuss the war with the presidents of Cameroon, Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Equatorial Guinea and Gabon.
The streets of Zaire's capital of five million people were crowded as Mobutu's motorcade swept to the airport. Many residents came out to watch and openly ask if he would ever return.
"The leopard is finished. He is not coming back," shouted an onlooker outside the aiport as Mobutu's plane took off.
Mobutu, who regularly sports a leopard-skin hat, was one of a handful of world leaders buttressed by the United States during the Cold War as a bastion against Soviet Communism.
With Kabila's rebels saying they have the teeming city in their sights, newspapers speculated that Mobutu, 66, would take advantage of the meeting to slip quietly into exile.
The independent La Reference Plus described Mobutu's departure as an "organised flight" linked to the rebel advance.

In Cape Town, Nelson Mandela, who hosted talks between Kabila and Mobutu on a South African ship in the Congolese port of Pointe Noire on Sunday, said he was satisfied Kabila was honouring a pledge to halt his army's march on Kinshasa.
But Kabila told Radio France International that taking the capital was "on the agenda" for the rebels. "Troops are obliged to advance," he said.
Kabila and his commanders, who took up arms in October in a dispute over Zairean nationality for minority Tutsis, have said they are building up for a final push against the capital.
But reliable reports from the battlefront were scarce and conflicting propaganda claims proliferated.

Zaire's government says its forces are battling to retake the town of Kikwit but independent sources say the belated army counter-attack was near Kenge, closer to Kinshasa. Rebel radio said on Tuesday it had driven back the counter-attack in a "brief but heavy encounter".
Diplomatic sources say the front line is close to the strategic Kwango River bridge 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.

In a sign of increasing tension, Air France diverted its scheduled flight from Kinshasa to Congo, on the opposite side of the Zaire river. An airline official said the plane normally stayed nine hours on the ground in Kinshasa, too long under current circumstances.
France has appeared squeezed out of the diplomatic manoeuvrings that have included a tour by U.S. envoy Bill Richardson and mediation by Mandela.

A retired French general arrived in Zaire's second largest city of Lubumbashi, rebel headquarters, for talks with Kabila, diplomats said. The French Foreign Ministry said Jeannou Lacaze, a former chief of staff of the French armed forces, was in Lubumbashi in a private capacity.
